50176:
Some prophecies point to a single fulfilment. Micah 5:2 names Bethlehem as the birthplace of a ruler whose origins are "from of old", and Matthew cites it for Jesus' birth (Matthew 2:5-6).

Others seem to be fulfilled more than once. **Isaiah 7:14** is the famous example. King Ahaz is terrified of two invading kings. Isaiah gives a sign: a young woman (Hebrew *almah*) will conceive and bear a son called Immanuel, and before the child is old enough to choose good and evil, those two kings' lands will be deserted (Isaiah 7:16). That sign had to mean something to Ahaz in his own lifetime. Yet Matthew 1:22-23, following the Greek translation that has *parthenos* ("virgin"), sees its full meaning in Jesus' virgin birth: God truly with us. Many evangelical scholars call this a dual fulfilment; others say Isaiah 7–11 as a whole already looks beyond Ahaz to a royal child (Isaiah 9:6-7), so Matthew reads the passage as a unit. The word "dual" is a label, not a biblical term; some prefer "near and far" or "typological" fulfilment.

Other examples: God's promise to David of a son whose throne would last for ever (2 Samuel 7:12-16) applies to Solomon and is applied to Jesus (Hebrews 1:5). Jesus' words in Matthew 24 mix the destruction of the temple in AD 70 with his final coming, and interpreters still debate how to divide them. Prophets often saw future events like mountain peaks from far away: two peaks that look side by side may in fact be far apart.
50178:
At Pentecost Peter says, "this is that which was spoken by the prophet Joel" (Acts 2:16, KJV). He quotes Joel 2:28-32, and even changes Joel's "afterward" to "in the last days". Some details, like the moon turning to blood, did not visibly happen that morning. Peter is not claiming every line was ticked off; he is saying, "this outpouring is the thing Joel spoke about; the last days have begun." Jewish interpreters of the time used a similar "this is" method: the Dead Sea Scrolls' commentary on Habakkuk says, in effect, "this refers to" events in their own community.

**Hosea 11:1** is the clearest case of pattern. "When Israel was a child, then I loved him, and called my son out of Egypt." In Hosea this is not a prediction at all; it looks back to the exodus. Yet Matthew writes that Jesus' return from Egypt happened "that it might be fulfilled" (Matthew 2:15). Matthew's word "fulfil" (*plēroō*) means "fill full". Jesus relives Israel's story: God's son, out of Egypt, through the waters, tested in the wilderness, faithful where Israel failed. The pattern is filled to the brim in him. Matthew 2:17-18 does the same with Jeremiah 31:15, Rachel weeping for her children.

This is what the learner means by "general-purpose" prophecy. Scholars call it typological or patterned fulfilment; Willis Beecher called some prophecies "generic", one promise fulfilled in a series of events that culminate in Christ. Some Catholic scholars speak of a *sensus plenior*, a "fuller sense" intended by God beyond what the human author saw. All of these are ways of saying that God's words carry more than their first moment.
50179: Conditional prophecy: when God's word is meant to change people
50180:
Jonah preached one sentence: "Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown" (Jonah 3:4). No condition was stated. Nineveh repented, "and God repented of the evil, that he had said that he would do unto them; and he did it not" (Jonah 3:10). Jonah was angry precisely because he knew God was "gracious... and repentest thee of the evil" (Jonah 4:2).

Jeremiah states the principle: if God announces disaster on a nation and it turns from evil, he will relent; if he announces blessing and it turns to evil, he will reconsider the good (Jeremiah 18:7-10). Many prophecies of judgement carry an unspoken "unless you repent". Micah's prophecy that Jerusalem would be ploughed like a field was not fulfilled in his day, and the elders later explained why: King Hezekiah feared the Lord and God relented (Jeremiah 26:18-19). Ahab's humility delayed judgement (1 Kings 21:27-29). Hezekiah was told he would die, prayed, and was given fifteen more years (2 Kings 20:1-6).

The Bible even records a prophecy adjusted in the open. Ezekiel foretold that Nebuchadnezzar would destroy Tyre (Ezekiel 26:7-14); later Ezekiel records that Nebuchadnezzar's long siege gained him nothing from Tyre, so God gave him Egypt instead (Ezekiel 29:17-20). Readers explain this differently (the prophecy was fulfilled in stages, later by Alexander; or it was conditional; or the prophet's word was revised), but the Bible does not hide it.

This matters for the test of a true prophet: "if the thing follow not, nor come to pass" (Deuteronomy 18:22). That test applies to unconditional words given as signs, not to warnings meant to produce repentance. A warning that leads to repentance has not failed; it has worked.
50181: Apocalyptic: visions, symbols and four ways to read them
50182:
Some prophecy takes a special form called **apocalyptic** (from Greek *apokalypsis*, "unveiling"). Daniel 7–12 and Revelation are the main biblical examples. Apocalyptic writing uses dreams, angels, numbers and strange beasts to unveil what is really happening behind history: the powers that seem to rule are beasts, and God's kingdom will outlast them all (Daniel 7:13-14). Revelation says God "signified" it (Revelation 1:1): it is told in signs. Reading these symbols as newspaper code is like reading a political cartoon as a photograph.

Christians read Revelation in four main ways (see the table below). **Preterists** say most of it was fulfilled in the first century, especially the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70 and Rome's persecutions. **Historicists** see it as a map of church history from the apostles to the end; this was the view of many Reformers and of Isaac Newton. **Futurists** place most of chapters 4–22 in a period still to come before Christ returns; this includes dispensationalists and many other premillennialists. **Idealists** read it as timeless pictures of the struggle between God and evil in every age. Many scholars today, such as G. K. Beale and Craig Keener, combine elements: Revelation spoke first to seven real churches, describes patterns that repeat throughout history, and looks to a real final victory.

Whatever approach you take, the centre of Revelation is the Lamb who was slain (Revelation 5:6). The Jesus lens matters here too: the conquering Lion of Judah turns out to be a slaughtered Lamb, and he conquers by his own blood and the faithful witness of his people (Revelation 5:5-6; Revelation 12:11).

50201: This is prophecy as God's word for the present: a call to covenant faithfulness, justice and trust. Ask what it asked of its first hearers, and what it asks of the church now. Most prophecy is of this kind.
50203: The word is meant to change people. If they turn, judgement may be withdrawn; if they turn away, blessing may be withdrawn. Its non-fulfilment is not failure (Jonah 3; Jeremiah 26:18-19).
50205: A promise that points beyond the prophet's day to a specific fulfilment, such as Bethlehem as the birthplace of the coming ruler. Check how the New Testament reads it.

50209: The New Testament sees God acting again in the same pattern, now at its climax in Jesus or the Spirit's outpouring. "Fulfil" here means "fill full". Examples: Hosea 11:1 in Matthew 2:15; Joel 2 in Acts 2.
50211: Many prophecies, such as oracles against Assyria or Babylon, were fulfilled in history and are not applied directly to later events. They still teach how God rules the nations and keeps his word.

50220: Jewish translators before Jesus rendered almah with parthenos, usually "virgin". Matthew quotes this Greek form.

50222: Matthew sees the fullest meaning of the sign in Jesus' virgin birth and translates the name: God with us.
50224: Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel.

50228: Follows the Hebrew word's normal meaning. The RSV's choice caused heated controversy in 1952; translators replied that Matthew's use of the Greek is still affirmed.
